Each stage one piston (1,2,3) fires with probability 1/3.  A ball’s fate depends only on its current platform position:
• In position 1 it is ejected with probability 1/3 (piston 1) and otherwise simply released – so P₁ = 1/3.
• In position 2 it is ejected immediately if piston 2 fires (1/3).  Otherwise it moves to position 1 and then has chance P₁.  Hence P₂ = 1/3 + (2/3)·P₁ = 1/3 + (2/3)(1/3) = 5/9 ≈ 0.556.
• In position 3 it is ejected immediately if piston 3 fires (1/3); if piston 2 fires it jumps to position 1 (chance P₁), and if piston 1 fires it moves to position 2 (chance P₂).  Thus P₃ = 1/3 + (1/3)P₁ + (1/3)P₂ = 1/3 + 1/9 + 5/27 = 17/27 ≈ 0.630.
New balls arrive on the platform either 1 at a time (after piston 1 fires) or 2 at a time (after pistons 2 or 3 fire). Therefore 40 % of new balls enter in position 2 and 60 % in position 3, giving every later ball an average success probability 0.4·P₂ + 0.6·P₃ = 0.6, which is still below 17/27.
The initial three balls start in positions 1, 2, 3 respectively, so ball 3 enjoys the highest possible probability of being struck by a piston.
Therefore, to maximize the chance of winning, pick ball number 3.

Let the three guesses (after ordering) be g1 ≤ g2 ≤ g3.
For any legal distribution the host may permute the boxes to minimise Bob’s gain.

Take the particular distribution (0,6,24).  The host can always assign the 24-coin box to g1 (yielding g1 coins), the 6-coin box to whichever of g2 or g3 is ≤ 6 (or, if both exceed 6, to either of them, yielding 0), and the 0-coin box to the remaining guess (yielding 0).  Thus Bob’s take against this distribution is at most
• g1 + g2  if g2 ≤ 6, or
• g1        if g2 > 6.
If g2 ≤ 6 then, because g1 ≤ g2 ≤ 6, the maximum possible total is 6 + 6 = 12.
If g2 > 6 then g1 ≥ 7, but against the distribution (6,12,12) every box contains fewer than 13 coins, so any guess ≥ 13 would earn nothing.  Therefore at least one guess must not exceed 12, meaning the previous case applies and again the total cannot exceed 12.
Hence no strategy can guarantee more than 12 coins.

Bob can actually secure 12 coins by guessing 6 for each box.  Whatever the distribution, at least two boxes contain 6 or more coins, so he receives 6 + 6 = 12 coins.

Each coin is worth $1 000, so the minimum amount of money Bob can guarantee is 12 000.
